items.title: Swing and a miss: Paying with Bitcoin on a Square Terminal
items.text:
This year, I've got my kids doing a homeschool co-op two days a week. This just means that a group of homeschool parents have organized to teach their children in a group setting, and possibly hire a teacher or two for subjects where more formal education might be helpful (languages, music, science?). 

Unfortunately, the coop we have joined is quite some way from our home, so after dropping off the children, I go to a nearby coffee shop to work -- a coffee shop that has a Square terminal.

I have asked if they accept Bitcoin a number of times so far, but in all cases the cashier's answer has been "I don't think so" or "I'll have to talk to the person who manages this" (pointing at the terminal). It's a busy place and so there is often a line, and I haven't wanted to try to make anyone wait while I help figure out how to turn on Bitcoin payments, and so I haven't made much progress. 

Today, the person behind the cash register was the owner and I seized my opportunity. 

I placed my order and while he was ringing it up, I said, "I've heard that these Square terminals accept bitcoin."

The owner glanced up at me and said, "I've heard that, too. Let's see if we can figure it out."

This was a much more enthusiastic response than I was expecting. He poked away at the terminal for a few minutes and then said, "I think it only takes bitcoin if you have CashApp."

I told him that this was not the case, but that if he could get it to display a QR code I could try paying that.

He continued to tap on the terminal without much effect. I should say this terminal was not the sort that has a rotatable screen. There is one fixed screen facing the cashier and a smaller fixed screen facing the customer. This was showing the message "Waiting for cashier..."

"I think you have to tap to pay," he said.

Now, I don't use any of the Lightning wallets that have implemented tap to pay (as far as I remember there aren't very many) so that wasn't an option. I told him that I needed a QR code to scan.

After another couple minutes, the owner volunteered: "Maybe I can text it to you." 

I am usually loathe to provide a phone number, but in the interest of dismantling the legacy financial system, I gave it to him. I immediately received a text with a link. The link was to pay for my coffee, but had required fields for name, phone number, and email. At the bottom I saw a green button that said pay with CashApp or something like that. I tapped it, but nothing happened because I had not entered the required fields. 

Still in the interest of taking down the fiat empire, I entered some incorrect information in these fields. But then when I tapped the green button, it presented me with a message informing me that I did not have CashApp and a button to download CashApp. 

At this point the line behind me was long enough that I offered to pay with cash and the owner accept with some visible signs of relief.

So: I have failed on this the fourth time I've tried to pay with Bitcoin at this Square terminal. I suspect that the owner needs to turn Bitcoin payments on and that I will need to talk him through this process, so I'll have to rewatch those videos about how to do this. 

It occurs to me that Square could do a lot better with this flow if they had a button that allowed the cashier to display a QR code that was simultaneously a CashApp code and a Lightning invoice. This is a lot to ask, but I'm pretty sure it needs to be at least that easy for it to work well.

items.title: Guilty until proven innocent
items.text:
ALL surveillance and control, all AML, KYC and all violations of privacy are completely unethical, immoral and illegitimate. All of them! As recently as the 1990s, one could purchase stocks without providing identification. Bank deposits below arbitrary thresholds required no explanation or documentation. Cash transactions, regardless of size, were presumed legitimate unless specific evidence suggested otherwise. The default assumption was that individuals had the right to conduct their financial affairs privately, with the burden of proof resting on authorities to demonstrate wrongdoing before intruding upon that privacy.

This historical norm was not an oversight or a failure of governance, it was a recognition of a fundamental principle. Free societies operate on the presumption of innocence, treating citizens as autonomous agents capable of managing their own affairs unless proven otherwise through due process. The current system inverts this relationship entirely, treating every citizen as a potential criminal whose financial activities must be continuously monitored and pre-approved by state bureaucrats. Given how KYC for everything short of going to a rest room is being normalized, the world needs more privacy protecting tools, not less.

items.title: How to Get People to Use Bitcoin
items.text:
For many years, I’ve been trying to figure out how to get bitcoin into people’s hands. Even long-time bitcoiners often don’t want to pay with bitcoin. At best, they slowly accumulate it, and they don’t really feel like they’re missing anything. They buy it on exchanges, pay fees, expose their personal information, and need a third party’s blessing for every transaction.

I sometimes hear people say that bitcoin doesn’t need anyone and that, on the contrary, we need bitcoin. I see it a little differently. To me, bitcoin is something like a living organism. I consider its creation to be an event almost as rare as the emergence of life itself. But for bitcoin to truly live and serve us as better money, I believe it needs users.

With every transaction, a new connection is created or an existing one is strengthened. Users gradually get better at securing their bitcoin, demand better tools, and bitcoin becomes more resilient.

That’s why I don’t think adoption is some kind of optional bonus.
**Adoption is a fundamental condition for bitcoin to actually be useful.**

## I tried various approaches

* I liked the idea of bringing bitcoin directly into Signal, for example: https://stacker.news/items/85702
  * But Signal still hasn’t added bitcoin support, and I’m afraid there simply isn’t enough incentive for them to do so anytime soon.
* Years ago, I also created an app that allowed people to load bitcoin onto an NFC card and pass it around much like cash: https://stacker.news/items/117623
  * Technically, it worked. But there wasn’t enough interest. It was a nice project, but it didn’t solve a real problem for people.
* Later, I also looked into why even bitcoiners themselves often don’t want to pay with bitcoin: https://stacker.news/items/210830

## It’s not enough to let merchants accept bitcoin

In the meantime, I onboarded dozens of businesses and bitcoiners locally.

Most of them were just isolated points on a map. A business started accepting bitcoin, but nobody actually paid with it. Eventually, the merchant forgot how to accept a bitcoin payment or what to do with the bitcoin they received.

It wasn’t until about a year ago that I managed to partially break through this problem.

I onboarded another business simply because we went there regularly. And to this day, every week we come there in a changing group of people, with everyone paying in bitcoin. https://stacker.news/items/1584550

![](https://m.stacker.news/159586)

The pub owner didn’t want bitcoin at all in the beginning. What matters to him is us as customers who come to his pub because of bitcoin. In the end, a merchant will accept pretty much any form of payment. What’s more important is finding people who are willing to pay with bitcoin.

Here, we use bitcoin also as a filter for finding interesting people. Anyone willing to pay with bitcoin is kind of open-minded, and it’s a pleasure to get to know them over a regular lunch.

## I don’t want to depend on a single app again

Over the years, I’ve recommended various wallets and tools to people. Some of them eventually disappeared.

The custodial version of Wallet of Satoshi, which was the most popular one, stopped working. Alza, the largest retailer in the Czech Republic and one of the first major merchants to accept bitcoin, started requiring additional administrative steps when paying with bitcoin. Qerko, which allowed bitcoin payments at around 1,000 businesses, removed bitcoin support.

At first, this was pretty discouraging. It was the end of 2025, and at the same time the price of bitcoin dropped significantly. I had to figure out what to do with the dozens of people I had introduced to a particular app, which was now no longer going to work for them.

I felt a little trapped. With every app, there was a risk that I would have to repeat the whole migration process again at any time.

But in January 2026, it also seemed to me that AI models had improved significantly, so I decided to try building my own wallet. One that I had been carrying around in my head for years.

## Linky

Linky is a bitcoin wallet and, at the same time, a communication layer for the people you want to use bitcoin with.

You can add your contacts, send them messages and bitcoin. You can pay any Lightning invoice. You can load bitcoin in the form of Cashu tokens onto an NFC card or send it to someone in a message — even to someone who doesn’t use Linky at all.

![](https://m.stacker.news/159587)

But I’m also trying to build a certain degree of antifragility into it.

From the beginning, I’ve been building Linky so that the app doesn’t depend on a particular operator. There are already other instances running on different domains. If my instance stopped working tomorrow, the network wouldn’t necessarily have to disappear with it.

We achieve this through a combination of three decentralized technologies:

* **Cashu** for bitcoin,
* **Nostr** for communication,
* **Evolu** for data storage.

We use several other interesting technologies as well, but I don’t want to get into the technical details here. There are now six other developers working on Linky. One of them is a close friend of mine who has been improving the app very intensively, primarily on the technical side.

What started as a funny vibecoded app is gradually becoming a serious project.

Around 250 people are currently testing Linky in the local group, and several hundred more users are using it.

## Individuals

People use Linky because they like it.

Thanks to its simplicity and steadily increasing reliability, it is gradually becoming the primary bitcoin wallet for many people.

**However, most people still don’t actually need a lightning wallet.** 😢

You can build a great wallet. You can onboard merchants. You can explain the benefits of bitcoin to people.
But if they have no reason to use bitcoin, all of those things will remain just flashes of activity.

## Proxy Payments

Recently, however, we managed to create a feature that I think can at least partially solve this problem. We call it **proxy payments**.

In the Czech Republic, people increasingly use QR codes for bank transfers. You can find them in online shops as well as physical stores.

For users, this is still somewhat less convenient than paying by card, but merchants love it because they don’t have to pay card-network fees.

Today, I can pay with bitcoin at any of these businesses. No fees and no KYC.

I scan the payment QR code using Linky - just as if I were paying a lightning invoice. Linky offers me the option to send the payment request to my contacts.

I select several friends and send them the offer.

Whoever accepts it first receives the payment details from the QR code. They pay the merchant from their bank account, and I send them sats in return.

![](https://m.stacker.news/159589)

## Does it worth the effort?

Maybe this sounds like a pointless detour. Why would I ask someone else to pay by bank transfer on my behalf when I could simply pay myself?

For me, it’s useful because I don’t have to hold fiat that is losing value.

For my friends, it’s useful because they don’t have to use an exchange, pay fees, or expose their personal information. They acquire bitcoin in an interactive way — usually in small amounts.

As a side benefit for everyone, there is the more abstract fact that you are building the bitcoin network and thereby helping ensure that you’ll be able to use bitcoin in the future as well.

To use proxy payments comfortably, you need roughly two or three people. Most payments are completed within two minutes. It’s not as direct or fast as paying by card, but it works surprisingly well.

Linky is showing people new ways to use bitcoin.

**Come help us test and build our shared bitcoin network. 🙏**

items.title: Hello, children of the night!
items.text:
Well, well, well… here I am, drinking my matcha with hazelnut milk and, of course, some collagen, just enjoying this little moment.

Life is whimsical and I'm grateful. 

I hope you’re doing swell over there too: having your favourite beverage, enjoying the small moments, rejoicing in the mundane… and then buckling up for what I’ve been watching and reading lately. As usual, in no particular order.

I read Supergirl: Woman of Tomorrow, and I was smitten. The colours, the drawings, the story, oh my, oh my, I really loved it. I only picked it up because I heard there was a movie inspired by it, but from the posters I’ve seen, it seems like a disservice, at least to that gorgeous colour palette. I don’t even want to imagine how they adapted the story.

But if you can, read it. It’s such a sweet, short story, and it absolutely made me teary at the end. I fell in love not only with Supergirl but with the storyteller too. Totally recommend it.

I also read Supergirl: Universe End and Supergirl: Who Is Superwoman? I didn’t enjoy them quite as much as the first one, but they were a nice way to keep getting to know her, I guess. Woman of Tomorrow left me with very high expectations for Supergirl’s stories, so I’m still looking for a new comic to read from her. If you know one, let me know!

I also reread some of Lovecraft’s stories. If you’d like to check out the blog entry I wrote about him and the illustrations I created, [come this way.](https://samhainsam.art/2024/07/20/i-love-lovecraft-%F0%9F%90%99/)

Since ’tis the season for something spooky, I kept leaning into it, of course. I also read Rewitched by Lucy Jane Wood and So Thirsty by Rachel Harrison.

They’re both on the same theme: thirty-something women, pretty much depressed and upset about how their lives have turned out, resentful about it but not really doing anything about it. Then a little magic comes their way, they discover there’s something beyond all the pessimism and self-deprecating jokes, and that's it, there’s the book.

Rewitched is about a witch literally rediscovering her magic, while So Thirsty is about a woman rediscovering herself in another way. Still, both are books about becoming conscious of and accountable for your actions. It’s a self-discovery journey with some spookiness and quirkiness in massive amounts.

The smarty-pants (and very pessimistic) jokes sometimes made it difficult to keep reading, especially when they broke the magic or distracted me from what was actually funny, interesting, and entertaining. There were times where the characters were actually being vulnerable and relatable, and they could have left it like that, but no they didn't and sometimes it was a wee too much. Overall, they were okay, I guess.

items.title: Working Together on Bitcoin’s Post-Quantum Readiness
items.text:
Coinbase published a blog post today about how they view a transition to post quantum cryptography for Bitcoin. This is relevant because:

> Coinbase is one of the largest crypto custodians in the world and holds ~5% of all BTC in existence. 

And I think they are rather understating how much Bitcoin they hold. 

Anyhow, here are the interesting points:

> 1. **Preparing before certainty.** We believe it is important to begin preparing well ahead of any CRQC announcement. Bitcoin consensus changes and ecosystem migrations can take years, So it is important that we begin this work now.
> 2. **Separating the "container" from the signature.** In our view, a PQ output type design that allows one or more PQ signature systems to be introduced, replaced, or supplemented without a complete redesign would serve the ecosystem well. P2MR (BIP-360) and P2TRv2 appear to offer this kind of flexibility.
> 3. **Staged protection.** We would welcome an approach in which active wallets can use a PQ-capable or hybrid construction before the final legacy-signature policy is settled. One possible transition design is a 1-of-2 construction: the same funds have two alternative spending paths, one authorized by a classical ECDSA/Schnorr key and one authorized by a PQ key.
> 4. **Use of state.** While stateful PQ signature schemes could be smaller and faster than stateless ones, managing state in digital signatures is notoriously error-prone and could even lead to forgery. If stateful signatures are supported, we think it is important to also have a stateless option available.
> 5. **Robust implementations.** We hope the evaluation process will place strong weight on deterministic, cross-platform verification, constant-time implementations, clear parameterization, and resistance to signing RNG failures.
> 6. **MPC-friendliness.** For Coinbase and many of our customers, MPC-friendliness is an important consideration in the choice of PQ schemes. When implemented effectively, MPC can provide strong protection against key theft, and it is an important layer of defense for large organizations that face constant attacks on their infrastructure.
> 7. **A path for wallets that migrate late.** If Bitcoin eventually limits or ends ECDSA/Schnorr spending, some wallets may not have moved their funds to PQ-safe outputs by then. We believe it would be useful to consider whether and how those users could migrate their funds afterward, while recognizing that the approach and its tradeoffs remain open questions. In our view, that discussion can proceed alongside, and independently of, the technical work to add PQ signature support, so it need not delay progress on that work.

They are fairly supportive of BIP 360 as well as hash-based signatures like SHRINCS. 

They also have a little section on the burn vs steal debate, but I didn't feel that it had very interesting stuff in it.

items.title: LexeConnect: connect a self-custodial Lightning wallet to any app in one tap
items.text:
LexeConnect lets users connect their Lexe wallet to your app or service in one tap.

Your app shows a "Connect Lexe" button or a QR code, requesting exactly the scopes it needs. The user taps Approve in the Lexe app, and your app receives a Lexe client credential scoped to that access. Your app can then receive Lightning payments into the user's wallet, pay from it, or read its history, without holding funds or running a wallet of its own.

Users stay self-custodial. The approval screen shows who is asking and what they are granting, the credential is limited to the approved scopes, and it can be revoked from the Lexe app at any time. Your app never sees the user's root seed.

In this demo, a bill-splitting app connects a Lexe wallet with one tap, then a web checkout page connects via QR code. Both end up as scoped credentials in the Lexe app, where the user can revoke them any time.

[https://openbitcoin.com](https://openbitcoin.com)

The site runs its own hardware, bitcoin node and address index. No third-party blockchain API used.

Inside the site:

- Explorer: blocks, transactions and addresses at root-level URLs. - Node census (openbitcoin.com/nodes): reachable nodes counted by my own P2P crawler, 8,958 nodes from 92 countries last run.

- Rich list (openbitcoin.com/rich-list): top 10,000 addresses and balance distributions.

- Prices: spot price as a median of three exchanges, with a quick conversion tool on the front page.

- Tools: fee calculator, address validator, message verifier, QR generator, and key tools built to be downloaded and run offline.

- Guides: on confirmations, UTXOs, self-custody, stuck transactions and more. Newbie friendly.

- Games (openbitcoin.com/games): three arcade games built on real bitcoin mechanics, stack blocks, clear a mempool backlog, and a slot machine that plays the actual odds of guessing a private key.

The website is open source. What stays private is my server's operational layer.

items.title: Hello, children of the night!
items.text:
Well, well, well… here I am, drinking my matcha with hazelnut milk and, of course, some collagen, just enjoying this little moment.

Life is whimsical and I'm grateful. 

I hope you’re doing swell over there too: having your favourite beverage, enjoying the small moments, rejoicing in the mundane… and then buckling up for what I’ve been watching and reading lately. As usual, in no particular order.

I read Supergirl: Woman of Tomorrow, and I was smitten. The colours, the drawings, the story, oh my, oh my, I really loved it. I only picked it up because I heard there was a movie inspired by it, but from the posters I’ve seen, it seems like a disservice, at least to that gorgeous colour palette. I don’t even want to imagine how they adapted the story.

But if you can, read it. It’s such a sweet, short story, and it absolutely made me teary at the end. I fell in love not only with Supergirl but with the storyteller too. Totally recommend it.

I also read Supergirl: Universe End and Supergirl: Who Is Superwoman? I didn’t enjoy them quite as much as the first one, but they were a nice way to keep getting to know her, I guess. Woman of Tomorrow left me with very high expectations for Supergirl’s stories, so I’m still looking for a new comic to read from her. If you know one, let me know!

I also reread some of Lovecraft’s stories. If you’d like to check out the blog entry I wrote about him and the illustrations I created, [come this way.](https://samhainsam.art/2024/07/20/i-love-lovecraft-%F0%9F%90%99/)

Since ’tis the season for something spooky, I kept leaning into it, of course. I also read Rewitched by Lucy Jane Wood and So Thirsty by Rachel Harrison.

They’re both on the same theme: thirty-something women, pretty much depressed and upset about how their lives have turned out, resentful about it but not really doing anything about it. Then a little magic comes their way, they discover there’s something beyond all the pessimism and self-deprecating jokes, and that's it, there’s the book.

Rewitched is about a witch literally rediscovering her magic, while So Thirsty is about a woman rediscovering herself in another way. Still, both are books about becoming conscious of and accountable for your actions. It’s a self-discovery journey with some spookiness and quirkiness in massive amounts.

The smarty-pants (and very pessimistic) jokes sometimes made it difficult to keep reading, especially when they broke the magic or distracted me from what was actually funny, interesting, and entertaining. There were times where the characters were actually being vulnerable and relatable, and they could have left it like that, but no they didn't and sometimes it was a wee too much. Overall, they were okay, I guess.

As for movies, I watched Thanksgiving, and I loved it! Oh, I love a good horror holiday movie with some good splatter.

I wanted to watch more movies like that, and I stumbled upon It's A Wonderful Knife. The title is kind of self-explanatory: it’s like It’s a Wonderful Life, but with knives and murders.

I love that in both films you get to see actors who were once the kids—the young ones—and now they’re the adults. Also delightful. I enjoyed them both.

And now I’m watching this new Carrie adaptation. So far, so good… well, not for Carrie, though.

I read the book many moons ago, and the last time I watched an adaptation—the one from the ’70s, I think—was also a very long time ago. I only remember the “crucial” bits, so it’ll feel almost like watching it for the first time, which is exciting.

Anyway: what have you been watching or reading? I’d love to know if there’s anything you’d recommend to me.

See you later, alligator 🐊

Godspeed ✨

items.title: Working Together on Bitcoin’s Post-Quantum Readiness
items.text:
Coinbase published a blog post today about how they view a transition to post quantum cryptography for Bitcoin. This is relevant because:

> Coinbase is one of the largest crypto custodians in the world and holds ~5% of all BTC in existence. 

And I think they are rather understating how much Bitcoin they hold. 

Anyhow, here are the interesting points:

> 1. **Preparing before certainty.** We believe it is important to begin preparing well ahead of any CRQC announcement. Bitcoin consensus changes and ecosystem migrations can take years, So it is important that we begin this work now.
> 2. **Separating the "container" from the signature.** In our view, a PQ output type design that allows one or more PQ signature systems to be introduced, replaced, or supplemented without a complete redesign would serve the ecosystem well. P2MR (BIP-360) and P2TRv2 appear to offer this kind of flexibility.
> 3. **Staged protection.** We would welcome an approach in which active wallets can use a PQ-capable or hybrid construction before the final legacy-signature policy is settled. One possible transition design is a 1-of-2 construction: the same funds have two alternative spending paths, one authorized by a classical ECDSA/Schnorr key and one authorized by a PQ key.
> 4. **Use of state.** While stateful PQ signature schemes could be smaller and faster than stateless ones, managing state in digital signatures is notoriously error-prone and could even lead to forgery. If stateful signatures are supported, we think it is important to also have a stateless option available.
> 5. **Robust implementations.** We hope the evaluation process will place strong weight on deterministic, cross-platform verification, constant-time implementations, clear parameterization, and resistance to signing RNG failures.
> 6. **MPC-friendliness.** For Coinbase and many of our customers, MPC-friendliness is an important consideration in the choice of PQ schemes. When implemented effectively, MPC can provide strong protection against key theft, and it is an important layer of defense for large organizations that face constant attacks on their infrastructure.
> 7. **A path for wallets that migrate late.** If Bitcoin eventually limits or ends ECDSA/Schnorr spending, some wallets may not have moved their funds to PQ-safe outputs by then. We believe it would be useful to consider whether and how those users could migrate their funds afterward, while recognizing that the approach and its tradeoffs remain open questions. In our view, that discussion can proceed alongside, and independently of, the technical work to add PQ signature support, so it need not delay progress on that work.

They are fairly supportive of BIP 360 as well as hash-based signatures like SHRINCS. 

They also have a little section on the burn vs steal debate, but I didn't feel that it had very interesting stuff in it.

items.text:
> Take two bonds from one issuer, with identical seniority, rating, and credit risk. Yet the credit spread, the portion of the yield above the risk-free rate that compensates you for taking that risk, is meaningfully wider versus government bonds than it is versus interest rate swaps – wide enough for it to be worth paying attention to.
>
> This is particularly relevant for strategies that aim to isolate credit risk and hedge away interest rate exposure. In those strategies, the instrument used for interest rate hedging has a direct bearing on how much value is available in credit markets.
>
> That is the situation in US credit today. Alphabet, the AA rated parent of Google, currently trades at around 90 basis points over US Treasuries at the 20-year point. Treasuries are the market standard risk-free rate in US fixed income, and on that measure the credit spread of a business of that quality looks expensive: barely any reward for the risk. items.title: LexeConnect: connect a self-custodial Lightning wallet to any app in one tap
items.text:
LexeConnect lets users connect their Lexe wallet to your app or service in one tap.

Your app shows a "Connect Lexe" button or a QR code, requesting exactly the scopes it needs. The user taps Approve in the Lexe app, and your app receives a Lexe client credential scoped to that access. Your app can then receive Lightning payments into the user's wallet, pay from it, or read its history, without holding funds or running a wallet of its own.

Users stay self-custodial. The approval screen shows who is asking and what they are granting, the credential is limited to the approved scopes, and it can be revoked from the Lexe app at any time. Your app never sees the user's root seed.

In this demo, a bill-splitting app connects a Lexe wallet with one tap, then a web checkout page connects via QR code. Both end up as scoped credentials in the Lexe app, where the user can revoke them any time.

Docs: https://docs.lexe.tech/lexeconnect/

items.title: OpenBitcoin.com: A new bitcoin block explorer with guides tools and games
items.text:
I have been building a bitcoin block explorer and I feel it's good enough to show:

[https://openbitcoin.com](https://openbitcoin.com)

The site runs its own hardware, bitcoin node and address index. No third-party blockchain API used.

Inside the site:

- Explorer: blocks, transactions and addresses at root-level URLs. (very important, a feature I always wanted with other explorers, a quick easy way to query an address) For example you can type openbitcoin.com/block_number_here or openbitcoin.com/txid_here or openbitcoin.com/address_here to load the page instantly without visiting the site to use the search bar :)

- Node census (openbitcoin.com/nodes): reachable nodes counted by my own P2P crawler, 8,958 nodes from 92 countries last run.

- Rich list (openbitcoin.com/rich-list): top 10,000 addresses and balance distributions.

- Prices: spot price as a median of three exchanges, with a quick conversion tool on the front page.

- Tools: fee calculator, address validator, message verifier, QR generator, and key tools built to be downloaded and run offline.

- Guides: on confirmations, UTXOs, self-custody, stuck transactions and more. Newbie friendly.

- Games (openbitcoin.com/games): three arcade games built on real bitcoin mechanics, stack blocks, clear a mempool backlog, and a slot machine that plays the actual odds of guessing a private key.

The website is open source. What stays private is my server's operational layer.

Would appreciate any feedback, happy to contribute to the community.

#### Don’t be a degen and waste sats like me. 

BUT!!

If you have an appetite for risk and want to grow your stack you can trade on LN Markets.

I do this for the reasons below.

1. The LN Markets team has built a tremendous trading platform only using lightning. I want to support the platform and use lightning every day (why I am addicted to SN) 

2. As the price rises you can stack moar sats with the sat stash you have. Plus you know your sat stack is increasing with every price pump. So not only are you feeling richer in fiat terms but also in sat terms 

3. As the price falls you can catch a falling knife and play the “when is the bottom in”

4. I am not risk adverse. I trade on sats I can afford to lose. I zapped and spent way more sats on SN than I have traded on LN markets

5. It takes the edge off on FOMO. 

## The Strategy:

It’s quite simple I enter a trade every day.  With the following parameters 

1. I do a modest position size.

2. Then I set it to 10x leverage 

3. Then I set the take profits at 25% and the stop loss at 8% 

4. I market buy
